title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 316: The Laughter Circuit: Roots of Social Mirth
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 316 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Laughter Circuit: Evolutionary Roots of Social Mirth

Paragraph 1. Laughter is one of the most universal yet physically unusual human habits. Unlike articulate speech, which requires careful brain planning, genuine laughter is an automatic sound controlled by deep, ancient brain centres. Across every society, infants laugh by four months of age, months before saying a single word. For centuries, philosophers such as Plato and Thomas Hobbes dismissed laughter as a cruel sign of feeling superior to others' bad luck. In The Comic Primate, neuroscientist Dr. Robin Dunbar overturns this gloomy view, showing that laughter evolved millions of years ago to unite communities.

Paragraph 2. Dunbar bases his theory on studies of great apes such as chimpanzees, bonobos, and orangutans. During wrestling games and tickling, apes emit rapid panting noises that signal the activity is harmless play rather than real aggression. Although ape panting sounds physically different from human giggles, both share the same brain triggers. Dunbar argues that primates normally build friendships through physical fur grooming. However, once early human groups grew larger than roughly fifty members, manual grooming became impossible because an individual can groom only one or two friends at a time without missing vital food gathering. Laughter thus appeared as 'vocal grooming', spreading warmth to many group members simultaneously.

Paragraph 3. Modern body measurements strongly support Dunbar's bonding theory. During hearty laughter, repeated chest muscle contractions release natural chemicals called endorphins into the nervous system, easing physical discomfort while creating calmness, trust, and closer group attachment. Sharing laughter literally changes group brain chemistry.

Paragraph 4. Still, Dunbar examines the less friendly side of humour as well. Laughter does not only connect people; it can also act as a wall. Close groups frequently share private jokes and mocking humour to show who belongs and push outsiders away. Furthermore, conversations reveal clear social rank: lower-status speakers laugh far more often at powerful people's comments than bosses laugh at theirs, using laughter as a safe diplomatic tool.

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

q6.text: How did early philosophers like Plato view laughter?
options: A. As an innocent baby habit with no meaning
B. As a medical cure for chest muscle pain
C. As a scientific signal used during hunting
D. As an unkind show of superiority over others

steps: Đoạn 1: Plato và Hobbes coi tiếng cười là dấu hiệu hả hê, coi thường nỗi bất hạnh của người khác.

q7.text: What did Dr. Dunbar point out about ape panting sounds?
options: A. They sound completely identical to adult human laughter.
B. They share the same brain triggers and social purpose as human laughter.
C. Apes only produce them when defending territory against enemies.
D. Apes have forgotten how to use them in modern zoos.

steps: Đoạn 2: Âm thanh khác nhau nhưng cùng cơ chế kích hoạt não và chức năng giao tiếp.

q8.text: Why did manual fur grooming fail in larger early human communities?
options: A. People lacked enough time to groom everyone without neglecting food.
B. Early humans preferred sleeping rather than sitting near friends.
C. Grooming caused painful skin allergies in larger camps.
D. Leaders banned grooming because it wasted daylight.

steps: Đoạn 2: Chải lông thủ công mất quá nhiều thời gian, ảnh hưởng đến việc đi kiếm ăn.

q9.text: What physical effect does hearty laughter cause in Paragraph 3?
options: A. It stops oxygen from reaching the chest muscles.
B. It forces people to forget recent conversations.
C. It triggers endorphins that lower pain and build social calm.
D. It raises blood pressure permanently for several days.

steps: Đoạn 3: Co thắt cơ ngực giải phóng endorphin giảm đau, tạo bình tĩnh và tin tưởng.

q10.text: What does Paragraph 4 reveal about laughter between people of different rank?
options: A. Powerful leaders laugh twice as often as their workers.
B. Lower-ranking members laugh more often to stay on good terms with leaders.
C. Managers forbid employees from telling any jokes during meetings.
D. Subordinates only laugh when nobody else is listening.

steps: Đoạn 4: Người cấp dưới cười nhiều hơn trước lời nói của cấp trên như một chiến lược ngoại giao an toàn.
